newsitem.title: JAPAN: Daiei sells shareholdings, halves profit forecast.
newsitem.headline: Daiei sells shareholdings, halves profit forecast.

text.p: Japan's largest supermarket-chain operator Daiei Inc said on Friday that it had sold part of its shareholdings in banks and a department store, which brought revenues totalling 20 billion yen ($183 million) to the company, to cover poor earnings.

Daiei also halved its forecast for parent current profit in the year to February 28, 1997, to 13 billion yen ($119 million) from its previous forecast. Daiei's actual parent current profit in 1995/96 was 25.04 billion yen ($229 million).
It attributed the weak performance to poor sales of food products in light of the recent food poisoning epidemic in Japan caused by the O-157 colon bacillus bacteria, a Daiei spokesman said.

The bacillus, which causes severe diarrhoea, vomiting and fever that often leads to liver complications, has been found responsible for a widespread food poisoning epidemic this summer in Japan that has killed over 10 people and made more than 9,500 people ill so far.
"The O-157 epidemic caused our profits to decline 2.5 billion yen ($22.9 million)," Daiei chairman Isao Nakauchi said in a news conference in Osaka.

Daiei's executive vice president Jun Nakauchi said at a separate news conference in Tokyo that bad weather earlier this year caused sales in outdoor goods to decline. The company is also burdened by costs related to restructuring in its group companies, the Daiei spokesman said.

Daiei said that in late August it sold about 80 percent of the shares it held in major Japanese department store Takashimaya Co Ltd, worth 14 billion yen ($128 million), to Japanese department store Printemps Ginza SA.

Printemps Ginza, which is wholly owned by Daiei, runs a department store in the posh Tokyo commercial area of Ginza and has business ties with Printemps of France. It did not have any stake in Takashimaya before the share purchase from Daiei but now holds a 3.4 percent stake.
"A business tie-up may be possible if the companies have some projects to agree on," said a Printemps Ginza spokesman.
Takashimaya is a prestigious department store which plans to open a huge outlet in October in another shopping district in Tokyo.

Takashimaya was also the focus of attention earlier this year because of the arrest of its officials on suspicion of violating Japan's commercial code by paying money to racketeers to ensure that its shareholders' meeting in 1995 would go smoothly.
Jun Nakauchi said he hopes the deal will give Printemps Ginza a chance to exchange information with one of Japan's oldest department stores.
A Takashimaya spokesman said, however, that the share transfer is unlikely to result in a business tie-up with Printemps Ginza as the character of the two department stores are different.
Besides shares in Takashimaya, Daiei sold shares in five banks, including Tokai Bank Ltd, Sanwa Bank Ltd and Sakura Bank Ltd, through which it does most of its financial transactions.
Daiei plans to buy back the bank shares as the sales were intended merely to take profits, chairman Isao Nakauchi said.

He also said the company had gone too far in its restructuring efforts, particularly in the transfer of employees to subsidiaries, and would call back 500 to 600 employees who are temporarily working at subsidiaries.
Reducing staff and increasing self-service at its stores has not been accepted by Japanese customers, he said. ($1=109 yen)
